title: Checkpoint: Trade and the Global Economy
objective: After this level you can explain why countries trade and how tariffs and exchange rates affect it.
summary: The Big Mac index tests purchasing power parity with burger prices. One imported washer ties the chapter together: comparative advantage, containers, tariffs, exchange rates, trade balance.

cards.headline: What can a hamburger tell you about a currency?
cards.body: Since 1986, The Economist has compared the price of a Big Mac around the world, as a lighthearted lesson in exchange rates. It's also a good way to pull this chapter together.

cards.headline: The burger test
cards.body: The idea behind it is purchasing power parity: exchange rates should drift toward the rate that makes the same goods cost the same in different countries. If a Big Mac costs less abroad, in dollars, than in the US, that currency may be undervalued; if it costs more, overvalued. Take it with a pinch of salt: one burger can't capture local wages, taxes and other costs of doing business.

mascot.line: Economics you can eat. Possibly the tastiest index ever invented.

cards.headline: One import, the whole chapter
cards.body: Follow an imported washing machine home. Countries specialize where their costs are relatively lowest (Level 72), so it may well be made abroad. Containers made shipping it cheap (Level 76). A tariff can raise its price, as importers pass the cost on (Level 74). A stronger home currency makes imports cheaper; a weaker one, pricier (Level 75). And it arrives as an import, counted in the trade balance (Level 73).

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: Why countries trade: both sides gain, even when one country is better at making both goods.
Why trade makes a country better off overall while some workers and places lose out.
How tariffs, exchange rates and container shipping change the price of an imported product.
Which explanations economists give for why some countries are far richer than others.

questions.prompt: Which idea does The Economist's Big Mac index illustrate?
questions.explanation: The index uses burger prices to illustrate purchasing power parity: exchange rates drifting toward equal prices for the same goods.

questions.prompt: A Big Mac costs less, in dollars, in Country X than in the US. What does the index suggest about X's currency?

options.label: It may be overvalued
options.rationale: Overvalued would mean a pricier burger than in the US.

options.label: It must be pegged to the dollar
options.rationale: The index says nothing about pegs.

options.label: It has the world's lowest wages
options.rationale: Wages affect burger prices, but the index can't tell you that ranking.

questions.explanation: A cheaper burger, in dollars, suggests the currency may be undervalued, though the index has real limits.

questions.prompt: From Level 72: in Ricardo's example, which good should England specialize in?

options.label: Neither, since Portugal is better at both
options.rationale: Being worse at both doesn't stop England gaining from trade.

questions.explanation: Cloth takes England 100 workers against wine's 120, so cloth is its relative bargain.

questions.prompt: From Level 74: what happened to US dryer prices after the 2018 tariffs on imported washers?

options.label: They fell as shoppers bought fewer washers
They stayed the same, since dryers weren't taxed
options.rationale: They weren't taxed, yet their prices still rose.

options.label: They rose about as much as washer prices
They doubled overnight
options.rationale: They rose by about the same 12% as washers, not double.

questions.explanation: Dryers had no tariff, but their prices rose by about as much as washers', since the two are often bought together.

questions.prompt: Your home currency strengthens. Other things equal, what happens to the price of that imported washing machine?

options.label: It tends to rise
options.rationale: A weaker currency would make it pricier.

options.label: It is fixed by the tariff
options.rationale: A tariff adds a tax; it doesn't freeze the price.

options.label: It depends only on the Big Mac index
options.rationale: The index is a lighthearted test, not a price setter.

questions.explanation: A stronger home currency buys more foreign currency, so imports tend to get cheaper.
